question: What is Islam's stance on global warming and caring for the environment?
answer:
This is the question as it is phrased to me. So we answer this question today, as usual, by dissecting the question.

Firstly, before we get to the quote-unquote traditional answer, we need to be very, very careful about assuming Islam always says something specifically. This is a phrasing that we need to think very carefully about. The only time that we can definitively say "Islam says something" is if the Qur'an is explicit and the ummah has agreed. Then we can say: Islam says Allah is the Creator, no problem. Islam says the Qur'an is the Book of Allah, no problem.

So a brother is asking, "What is Islam's stance on global warming?" as if all of Islam has agreed on one stance, and then as if I am the spokesperson, officially designated by Islam with a capital I, that whatever I say... And the reason I say this is because what happens is this good, simplistic assumption that whatever problem I'm facing, there's going to be one answer, one definitive answer, and the person in front of me will answer it and solve it because he has studied the Qur'an. And we have to be very, very careful in this regard.

Imagine if somebody said, "What does Islam say about the factors that break wudu?" And this is something the Qur'an talks about and the Sunnah talks about. Can anyone definitively answer, "Islam says these factors break wudu"? Or will they have to say what? There's difference of opinion. And by the way, all four madhhabs have a different list. Can you believe? All four madhhabs have a different list. So Muslims... alhamdulillah, Allah has allowed this ikhtilaf. There are narrations from the Sahabah: the ikhtilaf within Islam is a mercy.

So Muslims have differed over even things the Qur'an and Sunnah are explicit about, like the arkan of wudu and taharah. What do you think about an issue that didn't even exist when the Qur'an came down, global warming? And then you want to say, what is Islam's stance?

And I remember last month somebody asked me, texted me, and I'm not exaggerating, it's exactly what it is. They texted, and it was a group of students of knowledge and mashayikh and 'ulama: "What is Islam's stance on the right to bear arms, the Second Amendment?" As if all of us have to have the exact same opinion, and Islam is going to tell us whether we should be pro-Second Amendment or anti-Second Amendment. You understand, this question is problematic, and before I even try to attempt it, I need to make sure we understand.

And by the way, this is a joke here: if you really want to effect change in the pro-Second Amendment lobby, all you need to do is wear our traditional desi garb, thawbs, turbans and big t-shirts: "Muslims for the Second Amendment." All of a sudden checks and balances and background checks and everything will come. That is the most effective way to actually get some gun reform. We should start a group called Muslims for the Second Amendment, and then we appear like Muslims of other lands appear, and then we go and petition with our guns: "Muslims, Second Amendment! We want the Second Amendment!" And you will see, mashallah... Anyway, that's beside the point. That was a complete joke, by the way. That was a complete joke, just so that you're aware.

But my point is that we need to remove this understanding that Islam has a concrete answer on any question that comes to your mind. And it reminds me of something that we find in the books of history that happened to the Kharijites, the first sect that broke away. They kept on criticizing Ali radiyallahu 'anhu by saying, "We want the judgment of the Qur'an. In al-hukmu illa lillah. We want Allah's judgment; we don't want yours. We want Allah's hukm; we don't want your hukm. We want the Qur'an's verdict, not your verdict."

And it is narrated in the books of history that once Ali radiyallahu 'anhu called their leaders in Kufa, in the main masjid, and he called for a big copy of the Qur'an to be brought out. And in those days the mushaf was not this convenient little booklet. The mushaf was bigger than this desk, because it's written on camel parchment. The full mushaf, no exaggeration, is almost as large as this desk, three, four foot high, massive. People had to bring it out. They brought it out and they put it in front of Ali and the leaders of the Kharijites.

And what was their slogan? "We want the Qur'an. We want the Qur'an." So Ali said, "Qur'an, speak." Silence. "Qur'an, judge between us." Silence. "Qur'an, we want your verdict." Silence. Ali didn't say anything. One of the Khawarij said, "O Ali, the Qur'an is not going to speak back to you. Like, what's wrong with you?" So Ali said, "If the Qur'an is not going to speak back, how do you want me to judge by the Qur'an? What do you mean by the Qur'an? The Qur'an has to be interpreted by men. I have to interpret. Now I'm the leader, and I'm giving you the laws."

You see, the slogan was a simplistic attempt to negate Ali radiyallahu 'anhu. It sounds so good: "We want the Qur'an, we want the Qur'an." What do you mean? Who's going to decide what is the verdict about whatever issues are taking place? "We want the Qur'an" as a slogan doesn't translate into actual laws. And Ali radiyallahu 'anhu is saying: you are just a bunch of sloganeering people who don't have hikmah. You're causing fitnah and fasad. The slogan sounds good; it doesn't mean anything. Anyway, that's a separate tangent here.

Point is that when we say, "What does the Qur'an say? What does Islam say?" it's a bit of a trick question. Unless the Qur'an is explicit: yes, Allah created us; okay, we can say "the Qur'an said," no problem. Now you're asking about global warming: what does the Qur'an say about this, or what does Islam say? We have to be very careful about this. Rather, the way the question should be phrased is: is there anything in the Qur'an and Sunnah that modern scholars can use to discuss this topic? That changes the whole paradigm. Now you're bringing in the ijtihad of human beings.

This goes back to a hadith of the Prophet that he told to Ali when he was going on war, an expedition. He said, "When you go to this enemy tribe and they say they want you to judge them by the judgment of Allah, do not agree to that, because you do not know the judgment of Allah. But if they say they're willing for your judgment, then give them your judgment and seek Allah's help." Notice the difference here. No human being other than the Prophet ﷺ speaks on behalf of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, not even the Sahabah. That's why the hadith is clear. The Prophet ﷺ is saying to this companion: if you go to this tribe and they agree to reconciliation and they say, "We want Allah's verdict," don't say you will give them Allah's verdict. How do you know Allah's verdict? Rather say, "No, I will try my best to be fair and just," and then ask Allah for help, ista'in billah.

So similarly, when somebody has a modern question about this issue (what does Islam say about carrying weapons, what does Islam say about this and that), then it's a bit of a broad question. You have to rephrase it: is there anything in our Qur'an and Sunnah, is there anything the classical 'ulama have said about this issue? That's how it needs to be phrased.

Also, by the way, another point. And again, the reason I chose this question, frankly, was not to get to the answer, but to answer the question firstly, because we need to get over this simplistic mindset. Why am I concerned about this? Because once again, I want to teach ourselves tolerance. What happens is, sometimes an 'alim will give you an opinion, and it's a good opinion, but it's the opinion of an 'alim. It's not the Qur'an; it is not Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And we take that opinion and we consider anybody who dares disagree to be upon misguidance, evil. Even worse, all you need to do is look at sectarianism across the globe.

Once we understand that... Yes, sometimes the Qur'an and Sunnah is explicit, no problem. Most of the time in intra-legal disputes, sometimes even in advanced theological issues, it's not clear-cut, and that's why there's a difference of opinion. It's not clear-cut, and I've given examples about this.

So, another point: you are asking me, and my training is in Islamic sciences, about an issue that deals with modern sciences. Global warming is not a subject that is taught in any madrasa across the globe. So this also explains another issue we need to think about. As our Prophet ﷺ said, give everyone their due right. Do not ask a shaykh or an 'alim about a speciality beyond Islamic sciences, or else you will get into a problem. And usually the shaykh or 'alim might not even know; he'll give you the response, and he will also fall into a problem. And I've given many examples about this.

When there is an area of expertise, go to the expert. Don't ask me about investment advice. Don't ask me about modern theories of science. Even though, me personally, I actually have a degree in engineering, I have a minor in chemistry, I am, alhamdulillah, trained in sciences, still, it's not my area that I'm reading on. I'm not a professor of science; I'm a professor of Islamic studies. So also, give everybody their due, and learn from the mistakes of what happened in the Western world when their preachers and theologians became their scientists.

In our ummah, alhamdulillah, we never had what happened in medieval Europe. Why? Because our 'ulama knew their place, and our Ibn al-Haythams and al-Razis knew their place as well. The scientists knew their place; they didn't give fiqh and fatwas. And our fuqaha and 'ulama did not tell us what to believe about biology and medicine. We never had the inquisitions of medieval Europe. We never had the Pope tell Galileo that the earth is stationary and the sun goes around the earth. That's what the Pope, the Christian cleric, said to Galileo. Galileo is saying the opposite, right? Galileo is saying the earth goes around the sun, and the Christian church is saying, "No, we believe theologically that the earth is stationary, and if you say otherwise, we're going to burn you at the stake." And they literally had a stake, and they were going to burn him over there. And so Galileo, obviously... We don't want to do that, do we? So don't go and ask them questions.

We just gave a lecture a few months ago about what the Prophet ﷺ said. He said this: "You know your dunya better than I do." And this is about what happened in his time.

Now, what if there was a clash? In this case, the 'ulama of the Shari'ah and modern scientists need to come together and discuss amongst themselves. And the biggest example is the theory of evolution, which maybe one day I'll discuss, but if you listen to my talks online, you know it is something that needs to be discussed. It is a clash, you know, between what some Muslims believe and what some scientists believe. There seems to be a clash. There's no real clash, by the way. There's no real clash; the clash is in our understanding. There cannot be an actual contradiction between what is provable by science and what the Qur'an explicitly says. We firmly believe this. But there might be a clash because we haven't either understood science or understood the Qur'an.

So in this case we need to get the experts in evolutionary biology, we need to get the experts who understand what the Qur'an and Sunnah might imply with these wordings, and then come together, which, believe it or not, still hasn't happened. You would think it would have happened by now; it still hasn't happened. So each side needs to discuss with each other so that they can formulate what can and cannot be said.

Now, when it comes to this issue, after all of these disclaimers, which were more important than the actual response (that's why I chose this question), now we say: in my humble opinion, we can find some generic verses and hadith that can be applied for topics in this regard. This is my opinion and the opinion of some of the 'ulama of our times.

And as an educated person in this world as well, me personally (I'm not speaking as a person of knowledge, I'm speaking as a person who studied science), I think it is quite convincing that global warming is something that is proven by modern science. It's something that is pretty much the standard understanding of what is going on. And I don't find anything in the Qur'an and Sunnah that would be problematic for that. There's nothing in the Qur'an and Sunnah that problematizes the perception, or the theory, or even the fact, that what we are doing is causing an ecological disaster of the highest magnitude.

And that having been said, it is very easy to make a case. Don't say "the Qur'an says"; say it is possible for our modern 'ulama to say, which is what I'm doing. It's possible for modern 'ulama to make a claim to be ecologically conscious, to tell Muslims that a part of their worship of Allah is to take care of the environment. This is something that we can make a case for from the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

Why and how? The Qur'an ascribes a general role of stewardship, of taking care of other creatures and species, to mankind, and this is explicit in the Qur'an. Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala mentions in the Qur'an: Allah has put you in charge, Allah has given you authority over that which is in the heavens and earth. Whatever you have power over to do, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has put you in charge of it.

And Allah mentions in the Qur'an that we are mustakhlaf. And mustakhlaf, one of the primary meanings of mustakhlaf: you are the guardian, and you will be asked about what you are in charge of. And the term khalifa:

> إِنِّي جَاعِلٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ خَلِيفَةً

There are two main interpretations of this term. The one that we will mention now (there's another one that maybe one day we'll mention) is found in early Islamic tafsir: khalifa means Allah has put us in charge, just like the term khalifat Rasulillah, that he has been put in charge. So we will be asked about our environment.

And this is something that is very explicit: that taking care of the environment, taking care of the plants and animals around us, this is something that is an act of worship. Our Prophet ﷺ mentioned that whoever plants a tree (this hadith is in Bukhari), whoever plants a tree and that tree then grows up, any human or creature or animal that eats of that tree, it will be an act of sadaqah for this person. So this hadith clearly shows us that being green, or taking care of the environment...

As well, the famous hadith of the man, or in some versions the lady, an evil lady who lived a lifetime of sin, and she saw a dog that was thirsty, and she went down, she gave the dog water, and the Prophet said she entered Jannah. The Sahabah said, "O Messenger of Allah, Allah will reward us for taking care of an animal?" This is a hadith in Bukhari. "Allah will reward us for taking care of an animal?" And our Prophet ﷺ said, "In every living creature there is reward." In every living creature, whether it's a bird, whether it's an animal, whether it's a human being, taking care of any living creature, there is a reward. This is a hadith in Bukhari.

And the famous hadith in Musnad Imam Ahmad, that our Prophet ﷺ said: if one of you has a sapling, a small little plant (you know what you buy in Home Depot, the saplings there; when you put it in your backyard, that's called a sapling), if any of you had a sapling and the trumpet is blown, if you're able to plant the sapling before the trumpet reaches you, go ahead and do that. Meaning, think of the future. Even though there is no future after Judgment Day, the concept here is: think of the future. Make sure you are doing good in this earth.

And Allah criticizes destroying nature. This is explicit in the Qur'an. Allah criticizes... For example: when he turns away from the Qur'an, then his main effort is to cause fasad in the cultivation and the animals. He wants to destroy nature, we would call it, right? Allah is describing an evil person as if he's destroying nature.

And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala mentions in the Qur'an: do not cause fasad in the earth after everything is in good order. Now, of course, the primary meaning of fasad is to harm people, kill people, but destroying nature is a type of fasad. It's very explicit in the Qur'an: harming nature is a type of fasad.

Also, we have in the seerah of the Prophet ﷺ the famous incident of the Battle of Hunayn, when our Prophet ﷺ had surrounded the people of Ta'if and they were being stubborn. The people of Ta'if lived in a walled fortress, and their cultivation was outside the fortress. All of the crops were outside the fortress; the date palms were outside the fortress. One of the Muslims got the idea: let's burn their crops, which are outside the fortress. And so one tree was burned, or maybe more than one was burned.

But when you burn a tree, will it only affect the people inside? Who else will it affect? Animals. Who else will it affect? Nature. Who else? Think about it. When you destroy the whole plantation: the environment, but also future generations, other people that are eating from that tree. Destroying nature is very different. And it's the beauty here, subhanAllah... Anyway, let me finish the narration, then let me come back to this beautiful point here.

When the people of Ta'if saw that some Muslims were destroying the trees, they began begging: "Don't destroy the trees. I mean, we're having war, we're killing one another; don't destroy the trees. We beg you, for our blood and kinship, for our common cause, we are all human beings here. We beg you, don't destroy the trees." And our Prophet ﷺ gave a commandment to not destroy the trees.

Interestingly enough, in this case nature was more important than human life, because destroying the trees would have meant for two generations they don't have food. It's not just this group that's trapped there. When you burn the trees down, it takes 40 years for the tree to grow, for that whole crop. You're going to ruin the ground. We see what's happening in Australia: these people cannot plant now for another, Allah knows how long. That forest tree is gone; that soil is gone. So it's not just harming the living people. You're going to harm other people, you're going to harm innocents, you're going to harm future generations.

When the people of Ta'if begged, our Prophet ﷺ had mercy, and he forbade the Muslims: don't burn the trees. And you know what? They weren't successful back then. They left the people, they went back to Medina. They didn't harm the trees. Think about that.

So we can extrapolate from the Qur'an and Sunnah that we are told to take care of nature and think about our ecology and whatnot. And so for those who are interested in this field, **it is definitely something that we can say can be an act of worship: that we take care of the environment, we are environmentally conscious, we quote-unquote go green, we advocate causes that will diminish global warming.** If we do this with the proper intention, inshallah, there is no problem in saying the general texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah would facilitate this.

Before I finish this question, a very important disclaimer: we have to avoid the two extremes. What are the two extremes? The first extreme, which is common in one segment, is to take these modern, politically correct causes and to make them the end-all and be-all of the religion of Islam, to make these causes the most important. Because, you see, the first thing we've got to do is check: does the Qur'an forbid this, or is it neutral, or encouraging? In my humble opinion, as I gave you, we can find encouragement. Once we find encouragement, the next thing we've got to do: okay, it's encouraged, but where is it on the list? Is it on the most important list? Is it on very important? So where is it on the list?

And what we see is that some people prioritize these issues to the point that it eclipses iman in Allah, it eclipses 'ibadat, it becomes more important than Qur'an and dhikr. And that's a mistake. That is a big mistake, because you will not enter Jannah simply by being ecologically conscious while you don't do your huquq with Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. That is more important. I'm not saying it's either-or, but I'm simply saying the one who wants to get involved here should prioritize it the way that Allah has prioritized. Make sure they themselves are praying, make sure they themselves have the connection with Allah, and yes, now that they have enough energy, they can go and do something else, no problem. This is one extreme.

And by the way, we see this, I think, most obviously in the issue of meat. You know, I still haven't answered the meat question. I've gotten like 15 questions; I'm delaying the juicy meat even longer. Zabiha, non-zabiha: I still haven't answered it academically. One day I'll do that, inshallah. But we see this in the meat issue, where segments of Muslims are more concerned about how the animal was treated than how the animal was slaughtered, and halal and haram goes over how the farmer used to treat the animal more so than the procedure for the slaughtering of the animal. And how the farmer treated the animal is important, but much more important to pronounce a verdict is what? How the animal was slaughtered.

So you see what happens when you don't prioritize properly. So you have this movement that says if the animal was treated unethically, it is haram, regardless of how it was slaughtered. And if the animal was slaughtered properly, but it was in a cage, the chicken was in a cage, we will pronounce the verdict of haram regardless of how the animal was slaughtered. So fiqh for them changes because of political correctness, and that's not right.

We don't have to have either-or. We can encourage ethical treatment of animals, which we should do, and I've done this multiple times, and we can say, but it is obligatory to slaughter the animal properly. Right? You have a whole package deal here. But when you don't have your priorities straight, then something which is not the most important... It's important; nobody's denying it's important. But it's not the most important. The most important is that the slaughtering and feeding the animal should be pure. That is more important. If the farmer mistreats the animal, that's wrong. It's a sin. The animal will be able to complain on Judgment Day, believe it or not. The farmer might be punished for what he has done. But the meat is still halal for us. Now, you don't want to buy it? That's fine. But don't say it's haram. But we'll get to that issue.

Now, that's one extreme. What is the opposite extreme when it comes to these issues? Who can tell me? ... Exactly. Our brother is well aware of these debates, because he's intrinsically involved online, sometimes on both sides, I wonder. Our brother correctly points out the other extreme, which is typically from under-educated or zealous fundamentalist types of people. I'm sorry to be so stereotypical, but this is what it really is. It boils down to people who think they're defending the tradition.

And so anytime anybody comes and says, "Yeah, okay, you can be green in Islam": "Astaghfirullah! Imam al-Nawawi, did he say anything like this? Ibn Hajar, did he talk like this? Imam Abu Hanifa, did he mention shutting the light off when you leave the room? This is all you liberal bakwas people; all of you sell yourselves to the progressive modernists." And these people, they want to defend the tradition, and they've never studied it critically. They are just so sensitive.

And we understand, so many changes have gone on. Anytime somebody comes and wants to push the boundary a little bit, they just have a knee-jerk reaction: "Oh, that's it, what's next now? Everything is halal. Okay, you're going to say LGBT is halal." We're talking about being green; next step is automatically LGBT halal. That's the way their minds work. Any change is going to change everything.

And so if you dare come and say, "You know what, it's not un-Islamic to be green; on the contrary, if you do it properly, inshallah you will be rewarded" (I mean, I quoted you 10 evidences from the Qur'an and Sunnah)... Just because there was no global warming in the time of Imam al-Nawawi and he didn't talk about it, does it make it wrong to advocate being ecologically conscious? Well, according to this group, it is, because again, they're so cautious about any change that they are not willing to have any type of different discourse. And we see them all the time. And this is another problem. Point is, we are ummatan wasatan.

So to conclude (and inshallah we'll finish with one question today, because it was a long question): to conclude, the Qur'an and Sunnah do not have something explicit about global warming, but we can make an argument from the Qur'an and Sunnah that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala will reward us for being conscious of every living being around us. That includes animals, and that includes plants. We can also make an argument from the Qur'an and Sunnah that it is nice to be ecologically conscious, that we should think about the plants, just like our Prophet ﷺ did. He praised people who are planting plants. He himself took care of the plants outside of Hunayn, even in case of war. It is a very easy argument to make.

And given the fact that science is now pretty much definitive that we have caused damage to the environment, then we can say, and I'll conclude with this verse, Surah al-Rum, verse 41: it is not implausible to derive from a verse in the Qur'an that mankind can cause disasters in nature. Has anybody in the past done it? Not necessarily. But the wording allows for it.

What does the wording translate as? Fasad has spread. Fasad means any type of chaos, any type of harm, and global warming is a type of fasad. Zahara al-fasadu fil-barri wal-bahr: fasad has spread in the heavens and in the earth. Why? How? Bima kasabat aydin-nas: because of the results of what men have done. We have caused the fasad; we have harmed.

Now obviously, the primary meaning is civil war: because men are stupid, they're fighting one another. The primary meaning is you're killing one another because of what you are doing. But the Qur'anic wording allows that you can say that one type of fasad is ruining nature. This is literally in the Qur'an:

> وَإِذَا تَوَلَّىٰ سَعَىٰ فِي الْأَرْضِ لِيُفْسِدَ فِيهَا وَيُهْلِكَ الْحَرْثَ وَالنَّسْلَ

This is explicit: fasad is destroying the crops. So one type of fasad is global warming. And Allah is saying fasad is the result of what you yourselves have done. And this is something that we can apply to what we see around us.

May Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala grant us wisdom, grant us ikhlas, grant us sabr. May Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala make us stewards of this earth who will be able to answer to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala for the responsibilities He has given us.
